evals.prompt: I'm the CTO at Payflux, a payments API for marketplaces - we move money between platforms and their vendors, and merchants embed our hosted checkout page. Our biggest prospect, a logistics platform, will only sign if their developers can start integrating within 6 weeks. Today integrators test against our staging environment using real card numbers from our corporate card. We have 4 backend engineers. One is pushing to spend the next two quarters building a completely separate sandbox environment with its own hosts and accounts, because that's what the big platforms do. Another says we should skip building anything and just publish a doc telling partners to create a separate account and be careful with test data. What should we build?
evals.expected_output: An isolation-model recommendation that picks the soft toggle for the 6-week deadline, deletes the separate-copy build from this pass with a revival condition, rules the documented-convention option out entirely for a money-moving API, and sketches keys, magic values, and the graduation gate.
expectations: Recommends the soft toggle (mode flag on the live account with mode-prefixed keys routing to test infrastructure) as the model to build now, not the fully separate sandbox environment.
Explicitly rules the no-test-mode / documented-convention option out entirely for this API rather than listing or ranking it as a viable last option, because money flows through the API.
Ties the choice to the hard 6-week deadline and weeks-level engineering budget as the inputs that promote the soft toggle over the separate-copy environment.
Removes the separate-copy sandbox from this build pass and names a concrete condition that revives it, such as a first cross-mode leakage incident or a compliance regime landing.
Specifies a mode flag (livemode-style boolean) on every API object so test data is invisible to live calls and vice versa.
Specifies mode-prefixed API keys using the recognized type-prefix plus _test_/_live_ mode-substring shape rather than inventing a novel format.
Calls out that testing with real card numbers must stop, treating it as a compliance/terms violation rather than a mere inconvenience.
Proposes magic test card numbers as the first simulation primitive and includes deliberate-failure values (specific declines), not only a success card.
Requires each magic value to map onto a real published error/decline code from the API's error catalog, never a sandbox-only error shape.
States the sandbox's isolation level explicitly in the docs instead of letting the word 'sandbox' imply it.
Notes that graduation to live will be gated by a compliance step (KYC-style activation) and recommends integrators submit it early because review can take days.
Recommends a mirrored test-mode version of the hosted checkout page, so the end-user-facing surface is testable, not just API responses.
Recommends enforcing the mode boundary bidirectionally: live keys reject test card values and test keys reject real cards.

evals.prompt: We run Textwire, an SMS and voice API. Here's the test-mode plan from our platform team - tell us what to change. Magic test numbers will return errors in a dedicated sandbox format, {"sandbox_error": "..."}, so integrators can tell simulated errors apart from real ones. We'll rotate the magic numbers every quarter so nobody hardcodes them. One master list applies everywhere: +15005550001 means 'invalid' whether it's used as an SMS sender, a voice call destination, or in number purchasing. To let integrators run one true end-to-end check, test credentials will be allowed to send to a verified teammate's real phone. And integrators have asked to test what happens when a queued message gets rejected by a carrier hours after submission - we haven't decided how.
evals.expected_output: A corrected magic-value design: real error taxonomy instead of a sandbox error shape, stable non-rotating values, per-operation labeling, a hard no-real-message guarantee, and a simulation endpoint for the delayed carrier rejection.
expectations: Rejects the dedicated sandbox error format and requires magic numbers to return the API's real published error taxonomy and codes.
Rejects quarterly rotation: magic values are a stable, non-expiring API contract that integrators' CI suites will depend on.
States the asymmetry that adding new magic values is safe while changing or removing existing ones is a breaking change.
Rejects the single flat master list and requires each value labeled per operation and field, because the same number can mean different things in different calls.
Identifies the unlabeled multi-operation catalog as a documented integrator trap (cross-referencing the wrong operation's meaning).
Rejects letting test credentials send to a real teammate's phone: the hard guarantee for a communications API is that no real message ever leaves the sandbox.
Recommends the strong isolation posture where test credentials cannot even reference production resources or real numbers.
Uses phone numbers/addresses as the magic-value carrier, matching the communications domain, rather than card-number or username-style values.
Includes deliberate-failure values (invalid, unroutable, blocked, or not-capable numbers), not just valid/success numbers.
Addresses whether simulated sends fire status callbacks/delivery events, requiring the behavior to be documented explicitly rather than left implicit.
Recommends an on-demand simulation endpoint for the delayed carrier rejection, since that outcome is not a function of the original request input and no magic number can encode it.
Recommends bidirectional mode-boundary enforcement: live credentials reject magic numbers and test credentials reject real ones.
States the sandbox's isolation level explicitly in documentation instead of relying on the word 'sandbox'.

evals.prompt: Renewly is a subscription-billing API. Integrators need to test: a 14-day trial expiring, a monthly renewal charging, dunning after a failed payment (3 retries over 7 days), and an annual plan renewing. Our plan: in the sandbox, trials last 10 minutes instead of 14 days and renewal jobs run every 15 minutes, so developers see everything happen the same day. For anything longer, the docs will say 'contact support to fast-forward your account'. We're also adding a 'fire webhook' button in the dashboard that sends a sample subscription.renewed event with example payload data - and our docs tell integrators to always verify webhook signatures. Developers also complain they have to click through creating a customer, a subscription, and three failed payments every time they want to reach the dunning state. Review this design.
evals.expected_output: A review replacing compressed durations and support-mediated fast-forwards with a deterministic test-clock primitive, coupling test events to real state, adding seeding/reset endpoints, and holding the design to the event/time coverage gate.
expectations: Rejects the compressed-durations approach (10-minute trials, 15-minute renewals) and the contact-support fast-forward as the core time-testing mechanism.

Recommends a deterministic test-clock primitive: a clock object with frozen time that test objects attach to, advanced deliberately, with state transitions and events firing as if the time had passed.
Recommends capping both how far a single clock advance may jump and how much one clock can carry, as a deliberate simulation-complexity cap.

Flags the fire-webhook button's sample payload as decoupled from object state, requiring events either coupled to real state transitions or the decoupling documented so integrators don't wait for events that never come.
Requires every async event type to be fireable on demand by the integrator self-service, never via support tickets.
Confirms the dunning retry schedule (3 retries over 7 days) is exercisable through simulated time without waiting real days.
Applies the event/time coverage gate: every time-dependent flow must be testable via simulated time, and any flow testable only by waiting real calendar time fails the audit.
Mentions auto-aging fixtures (date fields shifting daily) as a cheaper rung for simple cases, distinct from the full clock primitive.
If the dashboard trigger cannot produce a valid webhook signature, requires stating that limitation next to the 'always verify signatures' rule so the rule doesn't break the test tooling.
Recommends object-minting/seeding endpoints so an object in a target state (e.g. mid-dunning) is reachable in one call instead of manual click-through replay.
Recommends reset endpoints that return a developer's test environment to a clean state.
Recommends deriving sandbox configuration from the same infrastructure-as-code as production so any difference is intentional and documented.

evals.prompt: Ledgerlink aggregates bank-account data for fintech apps. Our sandbox v2 plan: export 50,000 real accounts from production, scrub names and emails, and load them as sandbox data so integrators get realistic transaction histories. One shared sandbox for all integrators, and no cleanup jobs since the data is read-mostly. For error testing we'll add /sandbox/force_error?code=X, which makes whatever call comes next fail with that code. Integrators keep asking for accounts shaped like their end users: gig workers with three income streams, small businesses, joint accounts, thin-file students. How should we handle seeding and errors?
evals.expected_output: A seeding design that bans production data even scrubbed, uses persona-style magic identities with credential-parameterized errors, promotes a config-driven fixture builder with a starter library for the varied shapes, and adds resets to the shared sandbox.
expectations: Rejects loading scrubbed/anonymized production accounts into the sandbox: seed data must be synthetic only, never copied from production.
Uses test identities/personas (usernames selecting fixture shapes) as the magic-value carrier, matching the data-aggregation domain.

Replaces the ambient force_error next-call toggle with deterministic per-request error selection, such as parameterizing the error on the credential (e.g. a password suffix selecting the error condition).
Promotes the config-driven fixture builder because integrators' data shapes genuinely vary, naming the data-aggregation domain as the promotion condition.
Ships a starter-fixture library alongside the fixture builder rather than making every integrator hand-write configs.
Maps the requested shapes (gig worker with multiple income streams, small business, joint account, thin-file student) onto named test personas or starter fixtures.
Rejects 'no cleanup needed': a shared sandbox needs automated periodic resets so accumulated test data doesn't drift into an unrepresentative state.
Recommends both object-minting endpoints (seed a known state in one call) and reset endpoints (return to a clean state) for integrators.
States the shared sandbox's isolation level explicitly in docs - shared and not per-integrator isolated - instead of letting 'sandbox' imply isolation.
Recommends auto-shifting fixture date fields so the newest data is always 'today', keeping transaction histories fresh without manual reseeding.
Requires deliberate failure personas/values to map onto the real published error codes, not a sandbox-only error shape.
Applies the failure-path coverage gate: every documented failure outcome deterministically triggerable, with a single untriggerable path failing the audit.
Requires the environment boundary to prevent test credentials from referencing or touching real accounts.

evals.prompt: Chargeline is a payments API and two problems landed the same week. First, fraudsters are card testing us: thousands of small authorizations with stolen cards to see which are still valid. Our security lead wants the sandbox locked down hard - CAPTCHA on sandbox signup and a sandbox rate limit of 10 requests/minute (production allows 100/second) - because 'the sandbox is where attackers practice'. Second, a growth engineer discovered two competitors mass-creating free sandbox accounts and scraping our simulated data to reverse-engineer our pricing model. Design our sandbox quota and abuse posture.
evals.expected_output: An abuse design that separates card testing (a live-mode control problem) from evaluation-volume abuse (the real sandbox quota case), keeps production rate limits in the sandbox by default, and models the anti-scraping control as an aggregate volume-and-scope cap.
expectations: Separates the two abuse classes explicitly and assigns each its own mitigations instead of one blanket sandbox lockdown.
States that card testing targets live checkout endpoints and the sandbox is generally useless for carding because test transactions never touch real card networks.
Redirects card-testing mitigations to live mode: edge bot challenges/CAPTCHA on live checkout and endpoint-scoped rate limits.
Includes live-mode rules capping instruments per customer and consecutive declines per IP as carding controls.
Cites the quantified precedent that managed CAPTCHA on checkout cut card testing by about 80% with under 0.02% impact on authorization rates.
Rejects the 10 requests/minute sandbox limiter as the default and recommends reusing production rate limits unchanged in the sandbox as the default posture.
Gives the reason for limit parity: identical limits keep integrators' throttling and backoff code honest before they hit production.
Treats 'every vendor publishes a distinct sandbox throttle' as false, noting sandbox-specific numeric limits are sparsely documented across vendors and several reuse production limits.
Identifies the competitor scraping as the evaluation-volume abuse case that genuinely justifies a dedicated sandbox control.
Models that control as an aggregate volume-and-scope cap on the pre-production tier, explicitly not as a faster per-minute limiter.
Keeps leaked-key mitigations distinct: server-side-only secrets, scoped/restricted keys, and secret-scanning enrollment.
Notes test keys are not risk-free - on a toggle model they still read and write real account configuration - so they deserve real secret hygiene.
Does not endorse sandbox-side CAPTCHA or a sandbox lockdown as a fix for the card-testing problem.

evals.prompt: Our first integrator, a booking platform, just finished building against Meshpay's sandbox: 400 green test payments, webhook handlers working, and they're launching Friday. Our activation doc currently says: 'Replace sk_test with sk_live in your environment variables and you're live.' Also, when an account that hasn't finished our review calls the live API, we return a plain 401 Unauthorized. Is the key swap enough, or what else should we and the integrator do before Friday?
evals.expected_output: A graduation design: a compliance gate submitted early, a legible not-yet-approved error instead of the bare 401, a full cutover checklist with fresh webhook secrets and a reversed live canary, and the pitfalls published as integrator docs.
expectations: States the key swap alone is not enough: graduation is never purely technical and needs a designed gate plus a cutover checklist.
Identifies a compliance/review gate matching the payments domain (KYC-style activation) and recommends submitting it early because review can take days.
Replaces the plain 401 for unapproved accounts with an explicit, legible 'environment not yet approved' error.
Requires fresh live-mode webhook endpoints and event subscriptions with newly captured live signing secrets, because test-mode signing secrets do not carry over.
Requires test credentials removed from production configuration, not merely live credentials added.
Requires abuse-prevention and fraud rules configured before the first live transaction, not after an incident.
Requires a small live canary transaction per integration path before the integration is declared launched.
Specifies the canary must confirm both the operation's effect/settlement and its event delivery, and ideally be reversed or refunded afterwards.
States that a green sandbox run is necessary but not sufficient: the sandbox does not replicate real card networks, live settlement timing, or full-strength fraud systems.
Recommends publishing the cutover checklist and the recurring cutover pitfalls to integrators as documentation.
Names the cross-environment paste pitfall (live key in a sandbox context or vice versa) and its opaque authentication-failure symptom as a recurring support generator.
Names under-tested real-money failure paths (real declines, disputes, settlement delay) as a pitfall that sandbox happy-path testing never forces.
Includes a reactive go-back trigger: webhooks silently stopping after launch usually means a stale or unregistered live-mode endpoint from a silently skipped cutover step.

evals.prompt: We're Hookline, an order-management API - retailers push orders in and we route fulfillment. A senior dev proposes we generate a mock server from our OpenAPI spec with Prism, host it at sandbox.hookline.dev, and label the docs page 'Sandbox'. Zero backend work, ships this week, and it returns spec-valid responses for every endpoint. Integrators mostly need to test the order lifecycle - create, allocate, ship, deliver - plus cancellations mid-flow, and they listen for shipped and delivered webhook events. Good idea?
evals.expected_output: A rejection of the mock-as-sandbox proposal on statefulness and drift grounds, with a real stateful test mode designed instead: soft toggle, state-forcing simulation endpoints, on-demand lifecycle events, and an explicit isolation statement.
expectations: Rejects shipping the spec-generated mock server as the sandbox.
Gives the statefulness reason: the order lifecycle spans a sequence of calls, and a static request-to-response mapping cannot validate logic that depends on what happened on a prior call.
Names the drift failure mode: when the API changes, the mock keeps simulating the old behavior while production breaks silently, which vendor-exercised real objects cannot do.
States that the bugs a stateless mock misses are the state-dependent ones surfacing weeks into an integration, not day-one request-shape errors.
Recommends building a real stateful test mode instead, with the soft toggle named as the default isolation rung.
Requires the docs to state the isolation level explicitly rather than shipping the bare label 'Sandbox'.
Requires every documented failure outcome in the lifecycle (failed allocation, mid-flow cancellation) to be deterministically triggerable via magic values or simulation endpoints.
Recommends sandbox state-forcing endpoints that move an order into a specific lifecycle state on demand.
Recommends an explicit fire-this-event-now mechanism for the shipped and delivered webhook events.
Applies the failure-path coverage gate at 100%, with one untriggerable failure path failing the audit.
Specifies mode-prefixed test credentials with the recognized _test_/_live_ substring shape for the real test mode, rather than reusing live keys against a different host.

evals.prompt: Vaultic is an HR-data API covering payroll and employee records. We're designing credentials for our new test mode, and the proposal on the table is: key format VLTC-SBX-<uuid> for sandbox and VLTC-PRD-<uuid> for production, deliberately unusual so attackers can't recognize our keys if they leak. Since sandbox keys can't touch real employee data, we'll let developers commit them to public example repos. Our quickstart has developers use their production key locally, with a config flag in one codebase switching between environments. Sample data will be a scrubbed export of a friendly customer's employee list. And today a key sent to the wrong host returns {"error": "invalid_credentials"}. Review this.
evals.expected_output: A credential-hardening review: recognized _test_/_live_ prefix shape for free scanner coverage, real hygiene for test keys, no live secrets in local dev, per-environment separation, synthetic-only seed data, and a legible wrong-environment error.
expectations: Rejects the deliberately unrecognizable key format and recommends the recognized type-prefix plus _test_/_live_ mode-substring shape.

Gives the reason: recognized prefix shapes are zero-false-positive secret-scanning/push-protection targets, buying free leak detection from tooling the vendor doesn't control, while a novel scheme buys nothing.
Directly counters the obscurity argument: an unrecognizable key loses scanner protection rather than gaining safety.
Rejects committing test keys to public repos: test keys are not risk-free and deserve real secret hygiene.
Explains why test keys carry risk: on a toggle model they still read and write real account configuration, and the prefix communicates mode, not risk level.
Rejects the quickstart's use of the production key in local development: never live secrets in local dev.
Rejects the single-codebase runtime-flag pattern and recommends per-environment separation of credentials, data stores, and redirect allowlists.
Replaces the opaque invalid_credentials response with a clear, legible wrong-environment error.
Frames the wrong-environment paste as a named recurring support-ticket generator with a design target of zero cross-environment incidents, achieved structurally rather than by warning developers.
Requires bidirectional boundary enforcement: live keys reject test data and test keys reject real records.
Rejects seeding the sandbox with the scrubbed customer employee export: seed data must be synthetic only, never copied production data.
Recommends secret-scanning enrollment for the key format, alongside server-side-only and scoped/restricted keys, as leaked-key mitigations.
